house-robber-iii.d: Houses form a binary tree; you can't rob a node and its direct parent on the same night. Return the maximum you can rob.
house-robber-iii.i: DP on trees: each DFS returns a pair (best if this node is robbed, best if it is not). robbed = val + children's not-robbed; notRobbed = sum of max(child pair).

implement-queue-using-stacks.d: Implement a FIFO queue (push, pop, peek, empty) using only two stacks.
implement-queue-using-stacks.ex: push 1, push 2, peek -> 1, pop -> 1, empty -> false
implement-queue-using-stacks.i: Push onto an 'in' stack. For pop/peek, if the 'out' stack is empty, pour everything from 'in' into it (this reverses the order). Each element moves at most once: amortised O(1).

implement-trie-prefix-tree.d: Implement a trie with insert(word), search(word) and startsWith(prefix).
implement-trie-prefix-tree.ex: insert apple; search apple -> true; search app -> false; startsWith app -> true
implement-trie-prefix-tree.i: Each node has 26 child links and an end-of-word flag. Walk/create one node per character; search needs the end flag, startsWith doesn't.

insert-interval.d: Insert a new interval into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals, merging where needed.
insert-interval.i: Three phases in one pass: copy intervals ending before the new one starts; merge all that overlap it (min start, max end); copy the rest.

intersection-of-two-arrays-ii.d: Return the intersection of two arrays, with each value appearing as many times as it appears in both.
intersection-of-two-arrays-ii.i: Count one array in a map, then walk the other and take a value whenever its count is still positive (decrementing). If both arrays are sorted, two pointers need no extra space.
k: O(n log n + m log m)

intersection-of-two-linked-lists.d: Return the node where two singly linked lists merge, or null.
intersection-of-two-linked-lists.i: HashSet of nodes from list A works in O(n) space. O(1) space: walk pointers a and b; when one reaches the end, jump to the other list's head. They meet at the intersection (or both reach null) after at most m + n steps.
k: HashSet of nodes from list A

invalid-tweets.d: Return ids of tweets whose content is longer than 15 characters.
invalid-tweets.ex: content 'Let us make America great again!' -> invalid
invalid-tweets.i: WHERE LENGTH(content) > 15. (CHAR_LENGTH counts characters; LENGTH counts bytes. They're the same here since content is ASCII.)

invert-binary-tree.d: Mirror a binary tree (swap every node's left and right children).
invert-binary-tree.i: Swap children at each node and recurse. Pre-order or post-order both work.

is-graph-bipartite.d: Can an undirected graph's nodes be split into two sets so that every edge connects the two sets?
is-graph-bipartite.i: Two-colour the graph with BFS or DFS: give neighbours the opposite colour. A neighbour that already has the same colour means an odd cycle, so it's not bipartite. Start from every uncoloured node.

is-subsequence.d: Return true if s can be obtained from t by deleting some characters without reordering.
is-subsequence.i: Two pointers: advance through t and move the s pointer whenever characters match. s is a subsequence if its pointer reaches the end.
k: Recursive two pointers from the end

island-perimeter.d: A grid has exactly one island of 1s. Return its perimeter.
island-perimeter.i: Each land cell contributes 4 minus its number of land neighbours, so a plain double loop is enough. (Your BFS counts water or border sides per cell, which gives the same total.)

jump-game.d: nums[i] is the maximum jump from index i. Can you reach the last index from index 0?
jump-game.i: Walk backwards keeping a 'goal': if i + nums[i] >= goal, then i can reach it and becomes the new goal. Answer: goal == 0.

jump-game-ii.d: Same jump array; return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index (always possible).
jump-game-ii.i: BFS by windows: [l, r] are the indices reachable with 'jumps' jumps; the next window ends at the farthest i + nums[i] from the current window.

k-closest-points-to-origin.d: Return the k points closest to the origin.
k-closest-points-to-origin.i: Compare squared distances (no sqrt). A min-heap of all points then k polls works; better is a max-heap of size k (O(n log k)), or quickselect (O(n) average).
k: Min-heap of all points, poll k

koko-eating-bananas.d: Koko eats at k bananas/hour, one pile per hour (leftovers wasted). Find the smallest k that finishes all piles within h hours.
koko-eating-bananas.i: Binary search on the answer: speeds 1..max(pile). Hours needed = sum(ceil(p / k)) decreases as k increases, so find the first k with hours <= h. Watch for int overflow in the hours sum.

kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.d: Design a class that, after each added number, returns the kth largest number seen so far.
kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.i: Keep a min-heap of size k: it holds the k largest values and the top is the kth largest. Pop whenever the size exceeds k.

kth-largest-element-in-an-array.d: Return the kth largest element of an unsorted array (not the kth distinct).
kth-largest-element-in-an-array.i: Size-k min-heap: O(n log k). A max-heap of everything and k pops is O(n + k log n). Quickselect averages O(n).
k: Max-heap of all, poll k times

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.d: Return the kth smallest value in a binary search tree.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.i: Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order. Stop at the kth visit; an iterative stack makes stopping early easy.

largest-rectangle-in-histogram.d: Given bar heights (width 1 each), return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram.
largest-rectangle-in-histogram.i: Each bar's best rectangle extends to the previous and next smaller bars: area = h[i] * (nextSmaller - prevSmaller - 1). Find both with monotonic stacks, or in one pass: when a bar is popped, the current index is its next smaller and the new top is its previous smaller.
k: Previous/next smaller arrays via two stacks

largest-substring-between-two-equal-char.d: Return the length of the longest substring between two equal characters (excluding them), or -1.
largest-substring-between-two-equal-char.i: Store each character's first index; for each later occurrence the answer candidate is i - first[c] - 1. That's a single pass. (Your memoised interval recursion is O(n^2).)
